title: Attribute ledger movements to savings pots so a planned transfer is marked done by itself
description:
## What changes for the user
On payday the app lists the transfers the budget plans (to a pot, to a reserve line, to investments), and
each one stays "pending" until the person marks it done by hand, because the app cannot tell which
movement in the bank was that transfer. After this lands, when the money really moved into the pot, the
transfer shows as done on its own, with the day it happened, and the pot's page and the closing view agree
without a click. If it were wrong the person would see a transfer marked done that never happened (the
worst case: a month closed believing a reserve was funded) or one that happened and stays pending as it does
today.

## Outcome
This is a tracking bead. It holds the subject so it is not lost and tells whoever picks it up what was
decided, why it waits, what it will need from the write side and what must be decided first. It is not ready
to implement. It is finished when the open decisions below are answered by the person and written here,
including whether the balance history is long enough to attribute from, and the implementation beads exist,
each written whole and depending on the write side being complete.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database*
(`finwise.db`) holds what the person authors. *A pot* is a savings pot of a bank account (identity
`reserve:<account>/<reserveId>`, `investment:<id>`, or `slot:<account>/<n>` when the bank does not keep it
stable). *A transfer* is a planned movement derived from the month's budget: one per pot that has linked
provision or reserve lines (key `pot:<id>`, the sum of their amounts, named after the pot, or "Sem nome" for a
pot the bank gives no name), one per such line linked to no pot (`line:<id>`), and `investment` for the
residual above zero. *Marking* a transfer done is a write (`review.markTransferDone(month, key)`) stored per
month in `transfer_marks(month, transfer_key, done_on)`.

**What was decided.** A transfer is done only when marked by hand, for the month the screen shows. An
unknown or already marked transfer answers null.

**Decided by the person on 2026-11-23.** This item stays held until the measurement named under "Why it
waits" can be made, and decisions 2 to 7 below are taken with that measurement in hand. Two other courses
lost. Deciding all seven now, on the rule that exists: no case exists yet to say how often that rule is
right. Matching a movement to a planned transfer by amount and day alone, without the sightings: measured
the same day, an amount repeats within one account and month often enough to be unsafe for a mark that
feeds the month's closing.

**What the write side delivers that this builds on:**

- `transfer_marks` and the transfer keys above; a mark is a recorded change that can be undone.
- A pot's page shows its movements from the ledger only, and shows no synthetic deposit: a movement into a
  pot is not a transaction the API lists, because the transaction rules take the movements of savings pots
  out of the clean list (`internal/txrules`, `potmovements.go`).
- A movement is already placed on a pot, for the pot's page: `potrules.AttributeMovements`
  (`internal/potrules/movements.go`), called by `attachMovements` in `internal/api/pots_model.go`. The
  bank's row does not name the pot, so the rule reads the account's next sighting of its pots, at most
  three days after the movement: the movement belongs to a pot when that sighting holds that one pot only,
  or when exactly one pot's balance moved by the movement's amount since the sighting before. A pot that
  also earned yield in that interval does not match by amount, and its movement stays on the account. What
  does not exist is the step from a deposit placed on a pot to the planned transfer and its mark.
- A pot's contribution state on its page: closed; none planned when the current month's transfers have none
  for it; otherwise pending, or done with its day once marked. An investment pot follows the `investment`
  transfer.
- The net worth's contribution (planned, done, progress) comes from the current month's transfers and their
  marks; its investment rate is the budget's rate as planned, and the same rate as actual once the
  `investment` transfer is marked, zero before.
- A provision or reserve line counts as made, for its planned amount, in the closing view when the
  transfer that carries it is marked for that month or the month is closed.
- A `slot:` pot has an unstable identity, so anything attributed to it would not be stable either.
- `internal/potrules` also pairs and reads pot movements and balance histories for the yield.

**Why it waits, as measured on 2026-11-23.** The rule above applies only to a movement that is followed,
within three days, by a sighting of its account's pots. Over the real ledger the sightings around the
movements were too sparse for the rule to apply, so the measurement could not say how often the rule is
right, and in particular how often a pot's yield in the same interval keeps a deposit from matching. The
length of the history is therefore not the condition; that sightings are nightly around the movements is.

**The trigger to pick this up again:** the movements of at least one payday fall on days that are followed
by nightly sightings. Then run `TestPotRulesOverARealSnapshot` (`internal/potrules/realsnapshot_test.go`)
with `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` naming a current snapshot: its last log line counts the movements the rule
placed and the ones it left on the account. Show the counts to the person and take decisions 2 to 7 from
them. A real ledger is a person's whole financial history:
a real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name, document, id) is
ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be shown to the
person running the test and goes into no file; the test runs only when `FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a
file. Fixtures are invented.

**What an implementer must respect**: money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path;
every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant; an automatic mark is a recorded change
in the journal with its author (which author is part of the decisions below) and can be undone; a mark the
person made by hand is never overwritten by an automatic one.

## What must be decided first
Decided by the person who uses the app, since a transfer marked done feeds the month's closing.

1. **When the history is long enough.** Answered 2026-11-23: not a number of days. The condition is the
   trigger under "Why it waits"; until then the app keeps asking for the mark by hand.
2. **How a movement is attributed to a pot**: by amount and day against the planned transfer, by the change
   of the pot's balance, or otherwise; and how close is close enough (days, cents).
3. **What an ambiguous match does**: two plausible movements for one transfer, one movement for two
   transfers (two lines linked to one pot), a movement that is a yield or a withdrawal. Whether the app
   leaves the transfer pending and says why, or asks the person to confirm.
4. **How an automatic mark and a manual one coexist, and under which author the automatic one is
   journaled**: which wins when they disagree, whether an automatic
   mark can be taken back (it should be a journaled change like any other), and whether the person can
   unmark one.
5. **What happens with a `slot:` pot** (unstable identity): attributed never, or attributed within a day.
6. **What the `investment` transfer follows**: a movement in an investment pot, in a brokerage account, or
   both.
7. **Whether the past is filled in** (months already marked by hand or closed) or only the months from the
   change on.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every item of "What must be decided first" has an answer written into this bead by the person, or is
struck out with the reason; item 1 is answered (a condition, not a number), and items 2 to 7 are answered
after the measurement its trigger names, which prints only counts.
- [ ] The implementation beads exist, each written to the standard (self-contained, checkable criteria),
each depending on the write side's last piece.
- [ ] This bead changes no code: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` before and after, and no test is added, so
there is none to see failing.
- [ ] Done when: the decisions are recorded here, the implementation beads are written and ready, and
nobody mistakes the by-hand mark for something the app already infers.

## Tests
None: nothing is implemented here. The implementation beads must carry: a movement that matches a transfer
and marks it with its day; two movements and one transfer; one movement and two transfers; a manual mark
that stays; the undo of an automatic mark; a pot with no stable identity; the measurement over a real
ledger printing counts and fixed sentences only.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** none now (this bead edits only the tracker). When implemented, expect: `internal/potrules` (the
attribution), `internal/ingest` (where it would run), `internal/api` (the payday read, the pot page's
contribution, the net worth's contribution), `internal/authored` if a mark records its origin, and the
golden files of the reads that change.
**Reads only:** `internal/potrules/`, `internal/txrules/potmovements.go`, `internal/api/review_payday.go`,
`internal/api/pots*.go`, `internal/authored/`

Not statable in a few lines until the decisions are made.

title: Leave one lookup helper of each kind for the transaction writes and remove the type nothing produces
description:
## Outcome
The writes that name transactions share one set of helpers: one function that looks one transaction up
and refuses an id the list does not show, one that reads an id and a text from the arguments, and one
that resolves a selection of several ids. The type `readOnlyError`, which nothing produces, is gone.
Nothing a person or a client can observe changes: every answer, refusal, recorded effect and index row is
as before.

## Context
**Why.** The write handlers of `internal/api` were written by several pieces of work running side by
side, and three of them each brought their own copy of the same helpers. The copies are correct; the cost
is that a rule about looking a transaction up now has to be changed in up to three places, and the work
that makes a lookup refuse a snapshot the ingest has not taken in touches exactly these call sites. This
item is done after that work, on the code it leaves.

**The terms.** A *write* is a method of the API that changes what the person authored. A write that names
a transaction resolves it with `lookupTarget` (`internal/api/transaction_target.go`), which finds the
listed transaction for a provider id and gives it its key in the app's index (`indexListed`); *found* is
false for an id the list does not show. A *refusal* is the answer `refused` with a reason; `not_found` is
the reason for an item that no longer exists. A *selection* is several ids sent by one bulk write, which
is all or nothing: every id is found before anything is written.

**What is duplicated, read line by line.**
- `countedTarget` (`transaction_count_writes.go`) and `targetNamedBy` (`transaction_tag_writes.go`) have
  identical bodies: `lookupTarget`, the lookup's error passed through, `refuse(reasonNotFound)` when not
  found. `countedTarget` is called in `transaction_count_writes.go` and
  `transaction_reimbursement_writes.go`, and by name in four test files
  (`transaction_count_writes_test.go`, `transaction_reimbursement_writes_test.go`,
  `transaction_reimbursement_step_undo_test.go`, `reimbursement_candidates_test.go`); `targetNamedBy`
  is called in `transaction_tag_writes.go` and `establishment_writes.go`, and by one test that keeps
  calling it. A third copy of the same refusal is written inline in `setReason`
  (`transaction_history_writes.go`). These lists were read on 2026-11-23 and other work adds tests:
  take the callers from the code.
- Three writes call `lookupTarget` directly and answer null, not a refusal, for an id the list does not
  show: `setLine`, `confirmLine` (`transaction_line_writes.go`) and `undoHistoryStep`
  (`transaction_history_writes.go`). They are not copies and stay as they are.
- `twoTextArguments` (`transaction_line_writes.go`, three callers) and `idAndText`
  (`transaction_tag_writes.go`, twelve callers in five files) both refuse anything but two arguments and
  read each as text. Their one difference: when the second argument is not a text, the first returns the
  first text with the error and the second returns two empty texts. No caller reads the texts when there
  is an error.
- Three functions resolve a selection, each with one caller: `targetsNamedBy` for `addTagToMany`,
  `everyListed` for `excludeMany`, `findManyListed` for `setLineForMany`. They differ in ways the callers
  and the tests depend on:
  - *How the ledger is read.* `targetsNamedBy` interprets the whole ledger in one pass (`listedLedger`).
    `everyListed` calls the single lookup's read once per id, which reads the ledger's rows again for each
    id. `findManyListed` reads the rows once and interprets each month once.
  - *An id the list does not show.* The first two refuse `not_found` themselves; `findManyListed` answers
    a boolean and its caller refuses.
  - *Indexing.* `targetsNamedBy` indexes every row itself, after every id is found, and answers targets
    with their keys; the other two answer listed rows and their callers index while they write.
  - *Repeated ids.* The first two take each id once, the first occurrence; `findManyListed` leaves that to
    its caller, which passes `distinct(ids)`.
  - *The order of refusals in the line write.* `setLineForMany` must refuse an unknown id before a month
    that lacks the line, whatever their order in the selection.
- `readOnlyError` (`errors.go`) is a type a handler returned to decline an input while part of the app was
  read-only. No handler returns it any more. What is left is the type, its case in `classify` and one case
  of `TestHandlerErrorsAreMappedByClassWhateverTheMethod` (`refusal_test.go`). The error kind `read_only`
  itself stays: the router answers it directly for a server without a database of its own and for a
  method with no handler (`serveChange` in `writes.go`).

**What a single resolver has to keep.** Every id found before anything is indexed or written; each id
once, in the order given, first occurrence; `not_found` for the whole call when one id is not listed, with
nothing recorded and no index row added; for the line write, the unknown id refused before the missing
line; the rows found being the ones the single lookup finds, which
`TestTheSelectionFindsAndIndexesWhatTheSingleLookupDoes` pins for the whole-ledger pass. That test calls
`targetsNamedBy` by name: its call becomes the single resolver followed by the indexing the tag write
does, and what it asserts stays. The shape that
fits all three callers is a resolver that answers the listed rows and leaves indexing to the caller; which
of the two efficient readings it uses is the implementer's, as long as the ledger's rows are read once per
call.

**What the work this item waited for left.** `indexListed` now takes the request's ledger view and
refuses to index from a snapshot whose projected run is not the run the ingest took in last, with an
error the router recognises by identity (`errSnapshotNotTakenIn` in `transaction_target.go`): the router
then has the snapshot taken in and tries the write once more. A helper of this item passes every error
of the lookup and of `indexListed` through exactly as it got it. Wrapped so that `errors.Is` cannot see
through it, or turned into a refusal, that error would end the write instead of retrying it.
`TestABulkWriteOverTheNextSnapshotFindsThePostedRowUnderThePendingRowsKey` and the other tests of
`take_in_sequences_test.go` and `take_in_router_test.go` pin this for a selection and pass unchanged.

**Tests that pin the behaviour**, all in `internal/api`: for the tag selection,
`TestABulkTagTagsEachTransactionOnceAndItsUndoRemovesOnlyWhatItAdded`,
`TestABulkTagWithAnUnknownIDRefusesTheWholeCallAndTouchesNothing`,
`TestABulkWriteLeavesNothingEvenWhenItsCallerKeepsTheChange` and
`TestTheSelectionFindsAndIndexesWhatTheSingleLookupDoes`; for the exclusion,
`TestASelectionTakesTheReasonOnceOnEachOfItsTransactions`,
`TestOneUnknownIDRefusesTheWholeSelectionAndChangesNoTableOrTheIndex`,
`TestASelectionIsFoundWholeBeforeAnyOfItIsWritten` and
`TestUndoingASelectionGivesTheMonthsListBackAsItWas`; for the lines, `TestSetLineForManyIsAllOrNothing`;
and the write cases of the conformance suite with their committed effects files.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `countedTarget` and `twoTextArguments` no longer exist, their callers use the one remaining function
of each pair, and `setReason` uses the lookup helper in place of its inline copy.
- [ ] `setLine`, `confirmLine` and `undoHistoryStep` still answer null for an id the list does not show;
their tests pass unchanged.
- [ ] One function resolves a selection for `addTagToMany`, `excludeMany` and `setLineForMany`;
`targetsNamedBy`, `everyListed` and `findManyListed` no longer exist as three.
- [ ] That function reads the ledger's rows once per call, shown by a test that counts the readings for a
selection of three ids in two months.
- [ ] Every test named in the Context passes with no change to what it asserts; a test whose only change
is the name of a helper it calls counts as unchanged.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is
empty.
- [ ] `readOnlyError`, its case in `classify` and its case in `refusal_test.go` are removed, and a server
without a database of its own still answers `read_only` for a write, shown by the existing test of it
passing unchanged.
- [ ] The diff adds no exported name and holds only the files this item lists as edited; of the test
files, only `transaction_count_writes_test.go` and `refusal_test.go` change beyond the call of a helper
whose name goes away.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: one helper of each kind is left, every pinned test and every golden file is as it was,
and the dead type is gone.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/api/transaction_count_writes_test.go`: the readings of the ledger counted for one
selection. `reimbursement_candidates_test.go` already counts readings of the whole ledger by taking the
reading as a function, which is one way to count without an exported name.
- Integration, existing: the tests named in the Context and the write cases of the conformance suite,
passing without a change to their assertions.
- Golden: none moves.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/api/transaction_count_writes.go`, `internal/api/transaction_tag_writes.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_line_writes.go`, `internal/api/transaction_history_writes.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_reimbursement_writes.go`, `internal/api/establishment_writes.go`,
`internal/api/errors.go`, `internal/api/refusal_test.go`, `internal/api/transaction_count_writes_test.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_tag_writes_test.go`, `internal/api/transaction_reimbursement_writes_test.go`,
`internal/api/transaction_reimbursement_step_undo_test.go`, `internal/api/reimbursement_candidates_test.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/transaction_target.go`, `internal/api/settings_counterpart_writes.go`,
`internal/api/writes.go`, `internal/api/transaction_line_writes_test.go`,
`internal/api/take_in_sequences_test.go`, `internal/api/take_in_router_test.go`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `bin/ci`

Seven source files of one package and six test files, four of which change only where they call a helper
by a name that goes away. No store function, no contract type and nothing of
the interface is touched. The lookup itself (`lookupTarget`, `indexListed`) is read and not edited: it
belongs to the work this item waits for.

## Recovery path
Nothing stored changes. Reverting the pull request brings the copies back and nothing else.
close_reason: One helper of each kind is left for the writes that name transactions: targetNamedBy refuses an id the list does not show, idAndText reads an id and a text, and listedSelection resolves a selection, reading the ledger's rows once per call and leaving indexing to its caller; the copies and the error type nothing produced are removed. Verified by the gate on the branch after main was merged in, by no golden file moving, by every pinned test passing with its assertions unchanged, by two new tests (the readings counted; every bulk write finding its whole selection before it indexes any), by the author's twelve deliberate breaks and by four more in review: three killed by a named test, one judged to change no answer. One answer changes and is said in the pull request: an empty selection over a missing snapshot now answers ledger_unavailable from the bulk exclusion too.

title: Read the pots' yield history in one pass over the ledger instead of three
description:
## What changes for the user
The list of savings pots and the net worth screen take about a third of a second to answer before the
person's own machine or network is counted, and that will grow with the bank history. Most of that time is
spent reading the history of each pot's yield. After this lands, both screens answer in well under 200 ms
and show exactly the figures they show today.

## Outcome
The yield history of the pots costs one pass over the ledger's transactions, or none beyond the request's
own reading of them, instead of three passes of its own. No yield figure, no pot figure and no answer of
the API changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is an SQLite snapshot a
separate collector (pluggy-sync) fills from the banks; the app only reads it, through a view that is one
read transaction per request (`internal/ledger`). *A pot* is a savings pot of a bank account. *The yield
history* is what `(*View).YieldHistory` answers (`internal/ledger/yield_history.go`): for each pot and day,
what the pot earned, built from three readings named `readYieldTransfers`, `readYieldRemovals` and
`readYieldUnresolved` in the same file. The API attaches it to the pots in `attachYields`
(`internal/api/pots_yield.go`), on every read that loads the pots.

**What was measured, on 2026-11-23**, inside the server and over a real ledger, on one desktop machine;
durations and shares only. `savingsPots.list` took 339 ms and `netWorth.overview` 327 ms. Each read the
ledger's transaction rows once (about 80 ms), so the item that makes a request read those rows once takes
nothing from them. A profile of `savingsPots.list` put about two thirds of the time of loading the pots in
`YieldHistory`, split roughly evenly between its three readings: each costs about what one reading of every
transaction row costs. The person decided that day that a screen's read is slow above 200 ms inside the
server.

**What is not known yet, and is the first thing to find out.** Whether the three readings scan the same
rows three times, and whether what they need is already in the rows a request reads once
(`(*View).CleanTransactions`) or has to come from the tables directly. A query of `internal/ledger` that
mirrors one in pluggy-sync's README cites its lines in a comment, and such a query keeps meaning what the
README's means: if making the history cheaper would change what one of them mirrors, say so in the record
and stop there rather than diverge from the collector.

**What must not move.** The pots' yields are compared with the collector's own statement by tests over
invented ledgers and by an opt-in test over a real snapshot (`internal/api/pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go`,
`internal/potrules`). Money is integer cents; no float in the money path.

**What it waits for.** The item that makes one request read the transaction rows once (`finwise-vfw`): if
the yield history can be answered from that reading, it uses it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The record says, from the code, what each of the three readings scans and which of the two courses
was taken: one pass in place of three, or the request's own reading of the rows.
- [ ] `YieldHistory` answers, for every invented ledger of the tests, exactly what it answered before: a test
compares the two over the full invented ledger, and the tests of the pots' yields pass with no change to
what they assert.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is empty.
- [ ] A test counts the passes over the ledger's transactions that one `savingsPots.list` makes for its yield
history and finds at most one.
- [ ] The opt-in test of the pots' yields over a real snapshot is run **by the review, not by the
implementer**, and passes; the review measures `savingsPots.list` and `netWorth.overview` over a real
ledger, three runs each, before and after, and writes the durations alone in the pull request, saying
whether each is at or under 200 ms.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: the yield history costs at most one pass, every yield figure is as it was, and the review's
timings are in the pull request.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/ledger`: the yield history before and after, compared over the invented ledgers; the
count of passes.
- Integration, in `internal/api`: the pots list and the net worth over the invented ledgers, unchanged.
- Golden: none moves.
- Real ledger: only by the review, the existing opt-in test and the timings, durations only.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `internal/ledger/yield_history.go`, `internal/ledger/yield_history_test.go`, `internal/api/pots_yield.go`
**Reads only:** `internal/potrules/`, `internal/api/pots_yield_realsnapshot_test.go`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `bin/ci`

One file of the ledger's package with its test, and its one caller. The store, the contract and the
interface are not touched.

## Recovery path
Nothing stored changes. Reverting the pull request brings the three readings back and nothing else.

title: Show the history of answered proposals, each approved one with its undo
description:
## What changes for the user
An assistant on the command line can propose changes to the person's finance data, and the person answers
each one in the app with a yes or a no. Once answered, a proposal leaves the screen. If the person later
wants to see what they approved last week, why they refused something, or to take back a change they
approved days ago, there is nowhere to look: only the change made last can be undone from a screen. After
this lands, the weekly review has a list of the proposals already answered, each saying what it changed,
who proposed it, when it was answered and how, and an approved one can be taken back from there while
nothing later depends on it.

## Outcome
A screen lists the answered proposals, newest first: approved, refused (with the reason the person gave,
when they gave one) and stale. An approved proposal shows the change it made and offers its undo; an undo
the journal refuses says so with the sentence the app already has for it.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person, over a ledger snapshot a separate collector
fills from the banks; what the person authors is kept in the app's own database. *A proposal* is a change an
agent asked for through a command line: a method of the app's API, its arguments and a reason the agent
wrote. An agent never writes directly; the app applies a proposal when the person approves it. A proposal
for the budget line of a transaction still pending shows in the weekly review's queue as a suggestion; every
other one shows on the approvals card of the weekly review, with a view of the values before and after.
*Answered* means approved, refused, or stale: approved after what it would change had changed, so that the
usual refusal was answered and the proposal was closed. *The journal* records every change to what the
person authored, so that it can be undone.

**Why it was left out of the first version.** Decided by the person on 2026-11-23: the first version of
proposals has no history. The agent reads the outcome of its own proposals through its command, and the
person undoes a change right after approving it, with the toast every write has. Whether a history is
missed is only known with use; this item exists so that the screen is not forgotten.

**What it waits for.** The storage of proposals, the approvals card's backing and the difference view do
not exist yet. They are specified by `finwise-th6` and built by the items written from it. This item was
written before them, so the names of the table, of the read and of the screen's parts are not known:
whoever picks it up reads those items first and restates the criteria and the blast radius below against
what was built.

**What exists that it will use.** `changes.undo` (`internal/api/changes.go`) undoes a change by its id,
whichever it is, and answers the refusal `stale_change` when the journal refuses (`internal/authored/undo.go`);
the sentence the person reads for it is "Isso já foi alterado depois e não pode mais ser desfeito."
(`REFUSAL_SENTENCES` in `web/src/api/failures.ts`). The interface offers undo only for the change made last,
and no read of the API lists changes. The weekly review is `web/src/screens/revisao/WeeklyTab.vue`, with
`ApprovalsCard.vue` for the proposals that wait.

**Design.** The interface is ported from an HTML prototype (`design/README.md` says how), and the prototype
has no screen for this list. A design for it is needed before the screen is built, and it is the person's
to give or to approve.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A read of the contract answers the answered proposals, newest first, each with: what it proposed, in
the app's own words; the name its proposer gave; the reason the proposer wrote; the instant it was answered;
how (approved, refused, stale); the reason of a refusal when the person gave one; and, for an approved one,
the id of the change it made and whether that change can still be undone.
- [ ] The read answers an empty list, not an error, over a database that holds no proposal and for a server
without a database of its own.
- [ ] A proposal still waiting for its answer is not in the list.
- [ ] The screen lists them as designed and says in a sentence when there is none.
- [ ] The undo of an approved proposal calls `changes.undo` with its change; when the journal refuses, the
person reads the sentence for a stale change and the list is fetched again.
- [ ] The read has a case in the conformance suite, with a golden file over an invented authored state that
holds one proposal of each outcome, and the stand-in backend answers the same shape.
- [ ] The design parity passes for the new states on both viewports, with no limit raised.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: the person can open the weekly review, see what they answered and take back an approved
proposal from there.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/authored`: the listing over proposals of each outcome, newest first; a waiting one left
out.
- Integration, in `internal/api`: the read through the router; the undo of a listed change, accepted and
refused.
- Golden: one new file for the read over the invented authored state; none of the existing ones moves.
- Screen, in `web/src`: the list, the sentence for none, the undo and its refusal, over the stand-in backend.
- Parity: the new states on both viewports.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** `web/src/api/contract/review.ts`, `internal/contract/contract.json`, `web/src/api/fake/`,
`web/src/screens/revisao/`, `internal/api/review_approvals.go`, `internal/authored/`,
`internal/api/testdata/golden/`, `web/scripts/parity/states.mjs`
**Reads only:** `internal/api/changes.go`, `internal/authored/undo.go`, `web/src/api/failures.ts`,
`design/README.md`, `bin/ci`

One read, its statement in the store, one screen and its states. No write is added: the undo is the one
that exists. The file names are today's; the items written from `finwise-th6` decide where proposals live,
and this radius is restated against them before work starts.

title: Stop reading and interpreting the whole ledger on every call once its cost is measured to matter
description:
## What changes for the user
The app answers every screen by reading the bank's records from the start and working out what each row
means, each time. With the history the person has today that is fast enough that nobody waits; as the
history grows (a new month of purchases every month, for years) the time to open a screen, to save a budget
or to see a budget change while typing grows with it. After this lands, a screen opens as fast in the tenth
year as in the first, and a budget being typed answers as the person types. If it were wrong the person would
see it as a slowness that creeps in unnoticed, or, worse, as a speed-up that shows a number that no longer
matches the ledger.

## Outcome
This is a tracking bead. It holds the subject so it is not lost and tells whoever picks it up what was
decided, why it waits, what it will need from the write side and what must be decided first. It is not ready
to implement and should not be started until a measurement says it matters. It is finished when the
timings the write side's review took are written here, the person has said what is slow enough to matter,
and either this bead is closed as "not yet" with the date it is looked at again, or the implementation beads
exist, each written whole and depending on the write side being complete.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is the SQLite snapshot a
separate collector fills from the banks every night; the app only reads it. *The app's database*
(`finwise.db`) holds what the person authors. *Interpreting* a ledger is what `internal/txrules` does with
the collector's rows: it folds tax rows under their purchases, takes the movements of savings pots out,
marks movements between own accounts, bill payments, fees, refunds and unconverted amounts, and builds the
establishment key. *A snapshot swap* is the collector replacing the ledger file overnight.

**What was decided.** The cost of reading the whole ledger on every call is acceptable today and grows with
history, so it is deferred. The write side takes the timing of one write and of one draft evaluation on a
real snapshot, measured by the reviewer, in the reviews of the budget's arithmetic and of the transaction
writes, and that timing is what this bead waits for. (The plan states as its only open question the time of
one write and of one draft evaluation on the real snapshot.)

**Where the cost is, in the code as the write side leaves it:**

- *The ledger is reopened read-only on every call*: a handler gets a view with one handle and one read-only
  transaction on the snapshot, so every ledger query of a request sees one snapshot even if the collector
  swaps the file meanwhile. The reader opens the file per request; it is held nowhere.
- *Operations that span months interpret the whole ledger in one pass*: "all purchases here"
  (`transactions.applyLineToEstablishment`), the reimbursement candidates, and the card's own read, which
  also reach transactions older than the tracking start that were never indexed. A write resolves the
  transactions it names through the same interpreted read the lists use; the detail of one transaction
  interprets one month around it.
- *The count of what waits for review, on every screen* (added 2026-11-23, after the weekly queue landed):
  the frame of every screen and the home ask how many transactions wait for the person's review
  (`pendingCount` in `internal/api/pending.go`, answered by `shell.overview` and `home.summary`), and
  `pendingTransactions` there interprets the whole ledger whenever at least one review is kept, to leave
  out a review whose transaction the ledger no longer lists. It reads no ledger when no review is kept.
  It is one more cost to time with the others, on a database that has a review waiting.
- *The budget's arithmetic runs on the server*: the budget view sums a month's transactions into dispositions
  for every call, and the budget's edit mode and the scenarios screen call the evaluation on each change of
  the draft; those calls are not debounced today, and the plan adds a debounce only if the measured answer is
  slow enough to matter.
- *The index in the app's database* (`tx_index`) records observations to find a transaction's month, examples
  for the rules and its identity; it is never the source of any figure the screens show or sum. Using it to
  avoid reading the ledger would break that rule, and is therefore a decision, not an optimisation.
- *What the write side rejected, and why*, so it is not proposed again without the reasons: `ATTACH`ing the
  ledger to the app's database; copying the ledger into the app's database; opening a fresh ledger handle per
  query. The reason recorded for all three is that the reader hands out rows, never a connection, and the
  snapshot is swapped under it.

**Measuring, and what a measurement may say.** A real ledger is a person's whole financial history and this
repository is public. A real snapshot may be opened read-only; no value from it (amount, description, name,
document, id) is ever printed, logged, copied into a file, a commit, a bead or a pull request; a count may be
shown to the person running the test and goes into no file; the test runs only when
`FINWISE_LEDGER_SNAPSHOT` names a file. Fixtures are invented. A duration is not a value of the ledger, but
the size of the ledger is: a timing is recorded alone, never beside a row count or a number of months.

**What an implementer must respect**: money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path; a
cache must never show a figure that disagrees with the ledger the request opened, including across a swap;
every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant; every optimisation is proved by the
same checks that prove the thing it speeds up (golden files unchanged, the two invariants of the budget's
dispositions, the equality of the stand-in's answers over an empty ledger).

**Measured on 2026-11-23.** The write side's reviews had recorded no time per call, so the times were
taken that day: inside the server, over a real ledger, with a scratch database that held a budget and a
series of writes, on one desktop machine. Durations only.

| call | time |
| --- | --- |
| `review.closing` | 589 ms |
| `home.summary` | 575 ms |
| `review.weekly` | 474 ms |
| `settings.overview` | 386 ms |
| `savingsPots.list` | 339 ms |
| `netWorth.overview` | 327 ms |
| `budget.view` | 284 ms |
| `review.payday` | 195 ms |
| `transactions.detail` | 181 ms |
| `transactions.list`, one month | 180 ms |
| `card.overview` | 178 ms |
| `shell.overview`, asked on every screen | 177 ms |
| a write that looks a transaction up | 80 to 90 ms |
| `budget.save` | about 120 ms |
| `budget.evaluateScenario`, the draft | under 1 ms |
| one run of the ingest | well under half a second |

One reading of every transaction row took about 85 ms and interpreting the whole ledger on top of it 5 to
15 ms: the cost is the reading. The slow reads repeat it, up to six times in one answer. The pots list and
the net worth read the rows once and spend their time in the pots' yield history, which makes three passes
of its own.

## What must be decided first
Answered by the person on 2026-11-23.

1. **What is slow enough to matter.** A screen's read above 200 ms inside the server, and a write above
   150 ms, on the ledger and the machine of the measurement above. By that, seven reads are slow today, no
   write is, and neither the draft evaluation nor the ingest is. It is looked at again when the review of
   the first implementation item measures the same calls.
2. **What the review's timings were.** None per call had been recorded; the table above is the measurement.
3. **Which of the options is acceptable.** Removing the repetition, and only that: one reading of the
   ledger's rows per request, shared by every part of the answer, with nothing kept from one request to the
   next. Keeping the interpreted ledger in memory between requests is held back and decided only if a screen
   stays above 200 ms afterwards: it has to be invalidated when the snapshot is replaced, and what it can
   get wrong is a figure that disagrees with the ledger. Not taken: a debounce on the draft (the draft is
   not a cost on the server); interpreting incrementally; a cache in the app's database, since the index is
   never the source of a figure.
4. **How a cache is invalidated.** There is none to invalidate: nothing outlives a request.
5. **How it is verified.** No golden file moves and the conformance suites pass unchanged, which is the
   proof that every answer is the same; the times are taken again over a real ledger by the review, not by
   the implementer, and written as durations alone.

**The implementation items:** `finwise-vfw`, one reading of the rows per request; `finwise-c6t`, the pots'
yield history in one pass, for the two reads the first does not help, written with what is still to be
found out about its three readings.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The timings the write side's reviews took are written here, alone (no row count, no number of months),
and the person has answered item 1.
- [ ] Either this bead is closed as "not yet" with the date to look again, or every remaining item of "What
must be decided first" has an answer and the implementation beads exist, each written to the standard
(self-contained, checkable criteria) and depending on the write side's last piece.
- [ ] This bead changes no code: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` before and after, and no test is added, so
there is none to see failing.
- [ ] Done when: the cost is a measured number the person has judged, and either nothing is built because it
does not matter yet, or the optimisation is specified in beads that cannot show a figure different from the
ledger's.

## Tests
None: nothing is implemented here. The implementation beads must carry: the same answers (golden files,
equality over an empty ledger) before and after; a request across a snapshot swap that answers wholly from
one snapshot with the optimisation in place; the optimisation shown to be faster by a timing taken by the
review on the real snapshot, not by the implementer.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** none now (this bead edits only the tracker). When implemented, expect: `internal/ledger` (the
view and its lifetime), `internal/txrules` (what is interpreted and when), `internal/api` (the handlers that
interpret the whole ledger), possibly `internal/authored` if a cache is kept, and `web/` if a debounce is
added to the budget's edit mode and the scenarios screen.
**Reads only:** `internal/ledger/open.go`, `internal/txrules/`, `internal/api/budget_view.go`,
`internal/api/transactions*.go`, `internal/api/card.go`, `web/src/screens/budget/`

Not statable in a few lines until the options are chosen.
close_reason: A tracking item, and its own criteria are met. The times were measured on 2026-11-23 inside the server over a real ledger and are written in the item as durations alone. The person answered what is slow (a screen's read above 200 ms, a write above 150 ms) and which course to take: remove the repeated reading of the ledger's rows within one request, keep nothing between requests, and decide on anything kept in memory only if a screen stays slow afterwards. The implementation items exist: finwise-vfw and finwise-c6t. No code changed with this item.

title: Add a command-line interface for agents and the approval flow for the changes they or the model propose
description:
## What changes for the user
Today the person is the only one who changes anything in the app, through the screens, and the buttons that
exist for a change somebody else proposes (approve, refuse) do nothing: the approvals the screen is built to
show never arrive, because nothing is able to propose. After this lands the person can let an agent (an
assistant working for them in a terminal) read and change their finance data through a command, within
limits they set, and everything the agent proposes that needs a yes shows up in the app waiting for their
answer, with the reason, and can be taken back like any other change. If it were wrong the person would
find out as a change to their budget or to their transactions made by something that was never allowed to
make it, or as a request for approval that does nothing when they answer.

## Outcome
This is a tracking bead. It holds the subject so it is not lost and tells whoever picks it up what was
decided, why it waits, what it will need from the write side and what must be decided first. It is not
ready to implement. It is finished when the open decisions below are answered by the person, written into
this bead, and the implementation beads exist, each written whole and depending on the write side being
complete.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The app's database* (`finwise.db`,
created by `finwise serve --db`) holds everything the person authors. *The journal* is the record that
database keeps of every change (author, method, instant, effects), which is what makes a change undoable.
*A handler* is the function that answers one method of the API; the API's methods are listed in the
manifest `internal/contract/contract.json`, 82 of them, 56 of which change something (class `write` or
`evaluate`). *The approval flow* is the contract's `review.propose`, `review.approve` and `review.refuse`:
something proposes a change, the person sees it as an `ApprovalRequest` (`id`, `title`, `reason`: "a change
the model proposed that waits for a yes or a no") and answers yes or no. *The stand-in* is the in-memory
fake backend of the design prototype (`web/src/api/fake/`); it shows approvals as seeded data.

**What was decided.** The command-line interface and the approval flow are not part of the write side:
their shape and an agent's limits are a plan of their own. The write side makes the three methods exist and
answer null (nothing produces a proposal until the model or the command-line interface does), which the
interface already treats as "nothing happened". The monthly report's paragraphs can carry a `proposalId` and
a `sent` flag ("the suggested change is already waiting for approval"); nothing sets them yet.

**What the write side leaves ready for it:**

- *The handlers are meant to be callable outside HTTP.* Each write is a function over a recorder that
  already holds one transaction and the facts of the change (author, method, instant, Brazil day); HTTP is
  one caller of it. A command can call the same functions, with its own author and clock.
- *The journal's author is one of three:* `person` (an HTTP session), `rule` (the ingest) and `model`
  (reserved for the nightly call). An agent working through a command is none of these. Whether it is a new
  author, or acts as one of them, is open.
- *Every recorded change can be undone,* and an undo is refused as stale when what it would overwrite has
  changed since. That is what makes giving an agent write access reviewable: its changes are rows the
  person can list and take back.
- *Commands already exist in `cmd/finwise`* (`serve`, `hash-pin`, `backup`, `ingest`) with the repository's
  habits: exit 0 for success, 1 for a failure, 2 for a usage error; messages are fixed sentences that name a
  path and a reason and never the content of a file, because an SQLite error can quote a value; only
  `cmd/finwise` logs what the ingest or the PIN source did.
- *Access today is a session cookie* behind a PIN, over HTTP. A command has no session; how it
  proves it may act is open.
- The pot targets decision (see the tracking bead for pot targets) names this interface as the likely way to
  author the four Rainy Funds targets, since the design has no control for them.

**What an implementer must respect**: money is integer cents and no float may appear in the money path;
every SQL statement over the app's database is a registered constant and only `internal/authored` executes
it; the files of `internal/api` log nothing and read the clock only from the request; a real ledger is a
person's whole financial history, so nothing a command prints or logs holds a value from it that the person
did not ask to see.

**Corrections, read in the code on 2026-11-23.**

- Both items this one waited for are closed (`finwise-4ph`, `finwise-8kt`).
- No read lists changes: the contract of `changes` has only `undo`, which takes any change id, while the
  interface offers undo for the change made last only.
- An undo is refused as stale for more causes than a value overwritten since (`internal/authored/undo.go`),
  among them a row the undo would take along without restoring.
- The handlers cannot be called outside the router as they stand: the router builds their views, records
  the author `person` for every write (`serveWrite` in `internal/api/writes.go`) and holds the retry that
  takes a new snapshot in before a write.
- `review.propose`, `review.approve` and `review.refuse` are registered and answer null
  (`internal/api/review_approvals.go`); the approvals card exists on the weekly tab
  (`web/src/screens/revisao/ApprovalsCard.vue`) and its list is always empty.

## What must be decided first
Answered by the person on 2026-11-23, one point at a time. Each answer says what lost.

1. **The shape of the interface.** A thin client of the contract over HTTP, with three verbs: call any read
   by its name and print the JSON answer; propose (a method, its arguments, a reason); list its own
   proposals with the outcome of each. Exit statuses 0, 1 and 2, as the other commands have; the server's
   address and the token come from the environment. The read-only command is the first delivery.
2. **What an agent may do alone and what only proposes.** Nothing alone: an agent reads and proposes, and
   never writes directly. In the first version it may propose what belongs to a transaction (its line, its
   tags and its note, with the bulk and the whole-establishment variants) and also budget, subscriptions,
   exclusions, splits and reimbursements. Out of an agent's reach until the person says otherwise: closing a
   month, the PIN, settings. A proposal stores the method, its arguments and the reason the agent wrote; the
   app, not the agent, words what will happen, from the method; approving runs the same handler the screen
   uses, with its refusals. Lost: read only; direct writes for some classes of change with proposals for
   others (it needs limits per class, a screen to list and undo what an agent did, and more room to be wrong
   with the person's money); only line, tag and note; everything but the PIN.
3. **Who the author is.** A change applied from an approved proposal is journaled under the author `model`,
   which the journal already accepts, and carries the name its proposer gave: the person reads that it was
   proposed by that name and approved by them, and undoes it as any change. Accepting a suggestion in the
   queue stays the person's own change, as accepting the rule's suggestion is today.
4. **How a command proves it may act.** Over HTTP to the running server, with a token of the agent's own
   that opens the reads and `review.propose` and nothing else; the server refuses any other write for it.
   One token, made by a command and kept only as a hash in a variable of the server, as the PIN's hash is;
   revoking it is changing the variable and restarting. Lost: the PIN (a session equal to the person's, held
   back only by the agent's obedience); the command opening the database itself, as `finwise ingest` does
   (it works only where the files are and repeats what only the router does). A known limit: a process on
   the machine and under the user that owns the database file can open it from outside; the token guards
   the API, not that.
5. **How approvals reach the person.** A line proposed for a transaction still pending shows in the weekly
   queue itself, as the suggested line with the agent's reason, and the person accepts it or picks another;
   a pending review already carries `suggestion`, `confidence` and `justification`
   (`PendingReview` in `web/src/api/contract/transactions.ts`), the last null until something explains a
   suggestion. Everything else goes to the approvals card, with a view of the values before and after: the
   person asked for that view, a budget proposal needs it in any case, and it needs a design, since the
   prototype has none. A refusal closes the proposal and may carry a reason the person writes, which the
   agent reads. A proposal nobody answers stays, with no expiry; when what it would change has changed,
   approving answers the usual refusal and the proposal closes as stale. The card has an "approve all". The
   app applies an approved change, never the proposer. Lost: everything on the card (forty line proposals
   become forty loose sentences away from their transactions); a refusal with no reason; expiry after a
   number of days.
6. **How an agent is given its limits.** There is nothing to configure: the token only reads and proposes,
   and the list of what may be proposed is fixed in the server (item 2).
7. **Whether it authors the pot targets.** Struck out here: it belongs to the item on targets, `finwise-5xb`.
8. **How it is verified.** With invented data and the app's own tests, and one end-to-end test of the
   command against the real server over an invented ledger. Nothing is run against a real ledger.

**Left for later, with an item of its own:** a screen with the history of answered proposals, each approved
one with its undo (`finwise-moo`).

**Still owed before this item closes:** the implementation items, each written whole. A likely cut, to be
confirmed when they are written: the token and the read command; the storage of proposals with
`review.propose`, the command's propose and list verbs, and the approvals card backed for the proposals one
sentence describes; the line suggested for a pending transaction in the queue; the difference view, with
the budget proposal and the line of a transaction already categorised, after its design.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every item of "What must be decided first" has an answer written into this bead by the person, or is
struck out with the reason.
- [ ] The implementation beads exist, each written to the standard (self-contained, checkable criteria),
each depending on the write side's last piece, and none grants an agent a power the person has not given.
- [ ] This bead changes no code: `bin/ci` prints `CI green.` before and after, and no test is added, so
there is none to see failing.
- [ ] Done when: the decisions are recorded here, the implementation beads are written and ready, and the
three approval methods are not mistaken for finished work by anyone who sees them answer null.

## Tests
None: nothing is implemented here. The implementation beads must carry: an agent's change recorded under
its author and undone; a refusal when what the agent changed was overwritten; a proposal that appears,
is approved and applied exactly once; a proposal that is refused changes nothing; every output of a
command free of ledger values.

## Blast radius
**Edits:** none now (this bead edits only the tracker). When implemented, expect: `cmd/finwise` (the
commands), `internal/api` (the three approval handlers and what they store), `internal/authored` (a place
to keep a proposal, which means a migration owned by that work, and possibly a new author), the review
screens if an approval needs more than they show.
**Reads only:** `cmd/finwise/`, `internal/api/`, `internal/authored/`, `internal/contract/contract.json`,
`web/src/api/contract/review.ts`

Not statable in a few lines until the shape is decided.

title: Read the ledger's rows once per request and share the reading among the parts of an answer
description:
## What changes for the user
Opening the home screen, the weekly review or the month's closing takes about half a second before
anything of the person's own machine or network is counted, and the same wait comes back after every
change saved, because the screen loads again. It will get longer as the bank history grows. After this
lands, those screens answer in a fraction of that, and every figure on them is exactly what it was.

## Outcome
Within one request, the ledger's transaction rows are read from the snapshot file once, however many parts
of the answer need them. Nothing is kept from one request to the next, so every answer still comes from
the file as it is at that moment. No answer of the API changes.

## Context
**The terms.** finwise is a personal finance app for one person. *The ledger* is an SQLite snapshot that a
separate collector fills from the banks and replaces by renaming a new file over the old one; the app only
reads it. A request's *view* of the ledger (`internal/ledger`, `(*Reader).View`) opens the file at its first
query and keeps one read transaction until the request ends, so that every query of one answer sees one
state of the file (`Views` in `internal/api/views.go`). *The rows* are what
`(*View).CleanTransactions(ctx, period)` answers (`internal/ledger/transactions.go`); with the period
`wholeLedger` it answers every row. *Interpreting* turns rows into the transactions a list shows
(`txrules.Interpret`). *The app's database* holds what the person authors; it is not part of this item.

**What was measured, on 2026-11-23**, inside the server and over a real ledger, with a scratch database that
held a budget and a series of writes, on one desktop machine. Durations only: no value or count of that
ledger is written anywhere. One reading of every row took about 85 ms; interpreting the whole ledger on top
of it took about 5 to 15 ms. So the cost is the reading, and the slow answers are slow because they repeat
it:

| read | time | readings of the rows | of which reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `review.closing` | 589 ms | 6 | 497 ms |
| `home.summary` | 575 ms | 6 | 489 ms |
| `review.weekly` | 474 ms | 5 | 407 ms |
| `settings.overview` | 386 ms | 4 | 320 ms |
| `budget.view` | 284 ms | 3 | 236 ms |
| `review.payday` | 195 ms | 2 | 162 ms |
| `transactions.detail` | 181 ms | 2 | 161 ms |
| `transactions.list` (one month) | 180 ms | 2 | 161 ms |
| `card.overview` | 178 ms | 2 | 157 ms |
| `shell.overview` | 177 ms | 2 | 158 ms |
| `savingsPots.list` | 339 ms | 1 | 80 ms |
| `netWorth.overview` | 327 ms | 1 | 79 ms |

A write that looks a transaction up reads the rows once and took 80 to 90 ms.

**What the person decided that day.** A screen's read is slow above 200 ms inside the server, and a write
above 150 ms. The repetition is removed first, and only that: one reading per request, shared, with nothing
kept between requests. Keeping the interpreted ledger in memory from one request to the next was held back:
it is a cache that has to be invalidated when the snapshot is replaced, and the failure it can produce is a
figure that disagrees with the ledger, which is the failure that matters in this app. It is looked at again
only if a screen stays above 200 ms after this item, and decided then. A cache in the app's database lost
too: the index of transactions is never the source of a figure.

**What this item should take away,** computed from the table as the time of every reading after the first:
`review.closing` and `home.summary` about 410 ms each, `review.weekly` about 330 ms, `settings.overview`
about 240 ms, `budget.view` about 155 ms, and about 80 ms from each read with two readings. That would put
every read of the table at or under 200 ms except the last two, whose time is elsewhere: the pots' yield
history, which is the subject of `finwise-c6t`.

**Where the readings are, on `main` at the time of writing.** Take the inventory from the code; these are
the ones found:

- rows read whole and not interpreted: `shell.go` (the first month), `accounts.go` (the idle test),
  `review_payday.go` (the salary account);
- rows read whole and interpreted: `listedLedger` in `transaction_target.go`, called by `pending.go` (the
  pending reviews, behind `shell.overview`, `home.summary`, the queue and the closing),
  `subscriptions_charges.go`, `settings_counterparts.go`, `reimbursement_candidates.go` and
  `transaction_line_writes.go`; `card.go` (`loadCard`); `pots_model.go` (`attachMovements`);
- rows read whole to find one transaction: `findListed` in `transaction_target.go`, behind every write that
  names a transaction and behind `transactions.detail`;
- rows read for one widened month: `transactions_period.go`.

One request reaches several of these, each reading for itself. `reimbursement_candidates.go` already shares
one whole listing inside one call with `sync.OnceValues` (`sharedWholeListing`); that is the same idea at a
smaller scope.

**What makes it safe, and what could make it wrong.** A request's view is one read transaction, so a second
reading of the same rows inside it answers the same rows by construction: sharing the first reading changes
no answer. Two things could: sharing a reading across two requests (a request must never see rows another
request read, since the snapshot may have been replaced between them), and a part of the answer changing
the shared rows in place (sorting or rewriting a slice another part reads afterwards). Where the one
reading lives, in the ledger's view or in `Views`, is the implementer's choice, and so is whether a month's
rows are taken from the whole reading when it already exists.

**What a write needs.** A write's lookup compares the snapshot it reads with the run the ingest took in
last, inside its own change, and the router tries the write once more over fresh views after a take-in
(`indexListed` and `requireTakenIn` in `transaction_target.go`, `withSnapshotTakenIn` in `writes.go`). The
second attempt must read the file again: a reading shared within a request's view dies with that view, and
the tests of `take_in_router_test.go` and `take_in_sequences_test.go` pin it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Within one request the ledger's rows are read from the file at most once, shown by a test that counts
the readings for `home.summary`, `review.closing`, `review.weekly`, `settings.overview`, `budget.view`,
`shell.overview` and `transactions.detail` over the invented ledger with an authored state in which a
review waits: one reading each.
- [ ] Two requests read the file once each, shown by the same count; and with the snapshot replaced by
another invented one between two requests, the second request answers from the new one.
- [ ] No file under `internal/api/testdata/golden/` changes: `git diff --stat` over that directory is empty,
and the three conformance suites pass unchanged.
- [ ] A part of an answer cannot change the rows another part receives: a test changes the rows one caller
got and finds the next caller's as the file has them.
- [ ] The tests of `take_in_router_test.go` and `take_in_sequences_test.go` pass unchanged, and the second
attempt of a write after a take-in reads the snapshot the take-in left.
- [ ] Nothing outlives a request: no package-level variable and no field of the router, of the reader or of
the registry holds rows, shown by the test of two requests above failing when the reading is kept on the
reader.
- [ ] Each rule was seen failing once, by breaking it on purpose, and the record names the test that failed:
a second reading inside one request; the reading kept from one request to the next; a caller changing the
shared rows.
- [ ] The time of each read of the table is measured again over a real ledger **by the review, not by the
implementer**, three runs each, before and after, and written in the pull request as durations alone. The
review says which reads are at or under 200 ms and which are not.
- [ ] `bin/ci` prints `CI green.`.
- [ ] Done when: one request reads the ledger's rows once, no answer and no golden file changed, and the
review's timings are in the pull request.

## Tests
- Unit, in `internal/ledger` or `internal/api`, wherever the reading lives: one reading per view however
many times the rows are asked for; a new view reads again.
- Integration, in `internal/api`: the count of readings per request for the reads named above, through the
router; two requests; a snapshot replaced between two requests; a caller that changes its rows.
- Golden: none moves; the conformance suites of reads, authored reads and writes pass unchanged.
- Existing, unchanged: the take-in tests of the write side.
- Timing: none by the implementer; the review measures over a real ledger and prints durations only.

nothing of the interface is touched.

## Recovery path
Nothing stored changes. Reverting the pull request brings the repeated readings back and nothing else.
